# Freelance hourly rate calculator

Memtime helps you find those 30 minutes by automatically capturing what you've worked on and for how long.

[See How Memtime Helps You Capture More Billable Time](https://www.memtime.com/how-it-works)

## **What should I charge per hour?**

Answer the #1 question that determines your success as a freelancer

💰 For billing

![Grow profitability](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66ede8f3cf534f449306e1e3/69554c2cb3a65cefd047ed36_grow-profitability.png)

##### **Grow profitability**

To make your services profitable, you need to ensure you’re compensated fairly for the amount of work you put in. Calculate your hourly freelance rate based on your actual daily and annual workload, not just the vibes.

📊 For planning

![Improve estimates](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66ede8f3cf534f449306e1e3/69554cbbd4c6cf3baa6e8242_improve-estimates.png)

##### **Improve estimates**

Clients appreciate consistency. The price you quote in the beginning of a project should match the final invoice – otherwise your reputation suffers. Know your hourly rate ahead of time to make precise estimates and always stay within the scope.

💆 For wellbeing

![Get clarity](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66ede8f3cf534f449306e1e3/69554d07acd28120e0aa20fb_get-clarity.png)

##### **Get clarity**

If you’re unsure about your hourly rate or the number of hours you actually work, you won’t have the confidence to scale. Our calculator accounts for all your costs and expenses to give you the peace of mind to charge confidently.

## **Freelance pricing calculator**

As a freelancer, you need to consider many variables when determining your hourly rate. Our calculator is built to guide you and take all of them into account.

### **Annual salary target**

Your hourly rate is always tied to your annual revenue target. Your earnings as a self-employed consultant aren’t just the hours you work multiplied by your rate – it’s your total compensation including any time off and any overhead expenses you incurred.

Start by deciding how much you want to earn per year. Our freelance rate calculator will take that number into account to determine your ideal hourly rate.

‍

### **Annual time off**

When you’re self-employed, you’re in charge of your own schedule. Which means you can give yourself as much time off as you want – as long as it’s aligned with your salary target. To calculate your freelance hourly rate, you need to decide how many days a year you’ll be taking off work.

Our calculator excludes weekends by default, so you don’t need to worry about that. Only consider the vacation and holidays you’ll want to observe throughout the year and plug that number in.

### **Daily hours**

We all know how much we’re _supposed_ to work per day. But how much do we actually work? To get a reliable and profitable hourly rate, you need to be honest about the number of hours you work per day. This includes both billable and non-billable time, i.e. what you can put on the invoice as well as the costs you have to absorb as a self-employed person.

### **Billable hours**

Out of the total hours worked, billable hours is what makes it to the invoice. Any revenue-generating work for the clients is considered billable; however, every consultant has their own philosophy around calculating billable time.

For the purposes of this calculator, you need to consider the average daily hours you charge to your clients as their consultant. Not your ideal daily billable target but the actual number of hours you’re able to put on the invoice per day.

### **Business costs**

Anybody who’s run their own business knows that there are costs they can’t directly bill to the clients and have to therefore absorb. We’ve mentioned time off but what about the tools you use as a freelancer and any expenses such as hardware and software, office supplies, rent, utilities, etc.?

To calculate a valid hourly rate, you have to consider these expenses and distribute them evenly among your projects and clients if you want to stay profitable. Make sure to plug your annual business expenses into the calculator as well.

### **Time tracking method**

If there’s one thing that can dramatically impact the profitability of your freelance business without altering your workload, it’s the way that you track time and charge for it. For example, if you estimate your time, you can easily under- or overcharge clients because your memory is unreliable. Most freelancers who guesstimate their hours end up undercharging and overservicing clients.

## Practical guide: overdue invoice interest and how this tool works

Late payment interest is meant to reflect the cost of waiting for money you were entitled to on the due date. This calculator helps you turn dates, principal, and a chosen rate into a clear number you can put in front of a client or your own records. It is built for transparency: you see days overdue, daily accrual, and a written breakdown string that matches the math.

**What the math assumes.** Amounts here use **simple interest** on the original invoice total for the overdue window (from the day after the due date through the payment date you enter). Many statutory schemes and commercial invoices are quoted on that basis for straightforward debts. If your contract says interest compounds, accrues only on business days, or uses a different day-count convention, your real-world figure can differ—use this page as a structured estimate, then confirm against your paperwork or a qualified adviser.

### Choosing a fee type in the calculator

Each option maps to a different way clients encounter late charges in the wild:

- **Statutory rate** — Annual percentage applied pro rata over the exact number of calendar days overdue (÷ 365). Use the country chips for presets; you can still override the percentage if your reference rate changed.
- **Flat % of invoice** — One-time charge as a slice of the face amount, regardless of how long payment was late. Useful when your terms say “X% after Y days” as a single administrative fee.
- **Daily %** — The rate field is interpreted as a percent of principal _per day_ overdue. Common when agreements spell out a daily figure instead of an annual APR.
- **Monthly %** — The rate field is a percent per month; the tool approximates duration in months as days ÷ 30 for a practical running total. Compare that shortcut to your contract if it defines a “month” differently.

### United Kingdom: statutory interest in context

The Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 is aimed primarily at **business-to-business** debts on commercial contracts, not every consumer scenario. The headline formula most people quote is **8% per year plus the Bank of England base rate**, with the combined figure expressed as a simple annual rate and applied across the late period. The preset in this tool reflects a commonly cited total when the base rate is 5.25%; official tables and announcements change over time, so if your dispute spans a rate change, you may need to split periods or verify the rate that applied on each segment.

Creditors in scope may also have rights to **reasonable recovery costs** (including tiered fixed sums by debt size in many cases). Those add-ons are not modeled in the interest-only fields above—track them separately in your ledger and correspondence.

### United States: contract first, then caps

Unlike the UK statutory B2B framework, U.S. practice usually starts with **what you and the customer signed**: explicit late-fee or interest language on the quote, master services agreement, or invoice terms. Courts and regulators care whether the charge was disclosed, agreed, and not out of line with state **usury** or consumer-protection rules. The default U.S. preset here (18% per year, expressed as 1.5% per month in the interface note) is a widely used commercial shorthand—treat it as a starting point, not a 50-state guarantee.

### Australia: verify state limits and your agreement

Australian businesses often rely on contract clauses and, where applicable, **penalty interest** regimes that vary by state and by whether the debtor is a consumer or a business. The Australia preset uses a **10% per annum** simple rate as a practical ceiling-style reference used in many commercial discussions; your agreement, industry, or state law may prescribe something else. Always align the percentage with current local rules before issuing a final demand.

### Operational checklist before you rely on a number

1. Match the **currency** to the invoice and the bank account you expect to receive.
2. Confirm whether the due date excludes weekends/public holidays in your terms; this tool counts **calendar days** between the two dates you enter.
3. Keep a PDF or email trail of the original invoice, reminders, and any promise-to-pay messages.
4. If you use the demand letter block, replace every bracketed placeholder and attach your calculation screenshot or the breakdown text for consistency.
